summary: Jacob's descendants multiply and live in mutual support while Joseph remains alive, but Joseph dies after requiring an oath to carry his bones out of Egypt. Conflicts among rulers interrupt travel and ancestral burials, and a later policy portrays the growing Israelite population as a threat, imposes forced labor, and provokes Egyptian hostility.
whyItMatters: The chapter bridges Joseph's protected household and the enslavement of Israel. Its attention to bones, closed borders, and ancestral land keeps the prospect of departure alive even as conditions deteriorate.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: Egypt after Jacob's death, with royal wars involving Canaan and burial journeys to the ancestral cave near Hebron.
context.literaryForm: Generational transition, death and burial notices, royal-conflict summary, and an oppression speech.

before.text: Jacob has died, been buried in Canaan, and left the ancestral books with Levi. Joseph continues to oversee the family in Egypt.

here.text: The movement runs from mutual care and Egyptian honor to political suspicion, compulsory labor, and hatred after the older generation dies.

after.text: The next chapter recalls Moses' birth under a command to drown Israelite boys and the women whose care preserves him.

outline.heading: Growth and Joseph’s final command
outline.note: The family prospers in solidarity, and Joseph requires that his bones leave Egypt with them.

outline.heading: War, closed borders, and burial
outline.note: Royal conflict explains why Joseph is buried in Egypt rather than immediately returned to Canaan.

outline.heading: Burial of the brothers and renewed conflict
outline.note: Most bones are taken to the ancestral cave, some Israelites remain near Hebron, and Egypt’s gates close again.

outline.heading: Fear becomes forced labor
outline.note: The growing population is treated as a potential enemy and compelled to build cities and fortifications.

keyVerses.text: And it came to pass that after Jacob died the children of Israel multiplied in the land of Egypt, and they became a great nation, and they were of one accord in heart, so that brother loved brother and every man helped his brother, and they increased abundantly and multiplied exceedingly, ten [2242 A.M.] weeks of years, all the days of the life of Joseph.
keyVerses.why: The flourishing population is initially described through brotherly love and mutual assistance.

keyVerses.text: And he commanded the children of Israel before he died that they should carry his bones with them when they went forth from the land of Egypt.
keyVerses.why: Joseph’s command about his bones projects the family’s future beyond residence in Egypt.

keyVerses.text: 'Behold the people of the children of Israel have increased and multiplied more than we. Come and let us deal wisely with them before they become too many, and let us afflict them with slavery before war come upon us and before they too fight against us; else they will join themselves unto our enemies and get them up out of our land, for their hearts and faces are towards the land of Canaan.'
keyVerses.why: The royal speech turns population growth and ancestral attachment into a pretext for enslavement.

questions.question: What marks the period while Joseph is alive?
questions.answer: The Israelites grow and help one another, and the Egyptians honor them. The narrator gives this era an emphatically peaceful character before describing the death of Joseph and his generation.

questions.question: Why does Joseph require an oath about his bones?
questions.answer: He expects the Israelites eventually to leave and wants his remains carried with them. The explanation says Egyptian cooperation for an immediate burial in Canaan can no longer be assumed amid warfare and closed gates.

questions.question: Are all the brothers’ bones moved at the same time?
questions.answer: The later burial journey removes the brothers' bones but expressly leaves Joseph's behind. His oath therefore remains a future obligation after other ancestral remains have been returned.

questions.question: Who is “Amram thy father”?
questions.answer: The speaker is addressing Moses and identifies Amram as his father, among those who remain near Hebron. This direct address briefly makes the book's Sinai frame visible within its ancestral history.

questions.question: Why do the rulers fear the Israelites’ growth?
questions.answer: The speech imagines that they could join an enemy during war and leave because their loyalties face Canaan. It treats a growing resident population as a military threat and uses that fear to argue for slavery.

questions.question: What work are the Israelites forced to do?
questions.answer: Taskmasters compel them to build Pithom and Raamses and repair urban walls and fortifications. The text calls the service rigorous and evil, giving concrete form to the policy of affliction.

questions.question: Does their continued growth make the oppression harmless?
questions.answer: No. The narrator says they multiply despite harsh treatment, while continuing to describe slavery and Egyptian hatred. Survival and growth in the story do not reduce the wrong or burden of the forced labor.

glossary.def: Officials placed over the Israelites to enforce labor and affliction.
Harsh severity, describing the conditions of compulsory service.
Ancestral remains whose burial location links the family in Egypt with its promised departure and land.
